title: Nalanda
hookLine: the great monastic university of northern India, with thousands of students

cards: At the gate, a monk stops a young traveler and asks him a question. Not his name. A hard question about the teaching.
In the account of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, the keepers of this gate tested newcomers that way, and those who couldn't answer went home.

Whoever gets through steps into a world of monasteries, courtyards and lecture halls, crowded with students from near and far, and loud with debate. This is Nalanda, in the old land of Magadha in northern India.

teach.h: A MONASTERY THAT WORKED LIKE A UNIVERSITY.
teach.b: First, a place of learning. Nalanda was a monastery, but it worked like a university. Kings and patrons supported it, and monks lived, studied and taught there.
In the pilgrims' accounts, the days were full of lectures and debate. Second, more than one subject.
Students learned the sutras, Mahayana and older teachings alike, and also logic, grammar and medicine, the tools for reading and arguing well. Debate wasn't a sideline.
It was how an idea was tested, the way Nagasena and the king tested theirs. Third, the teachers. Tradition links Nalanda with well-known names.

Xuanzang's own teacher there was the abbot Shilabhadra. Tibetan tradition says the poet-monk Shantideva lived at Nalanda and recited his Way of the Bodhisattva there, to monks who had thought him lazy.
Some traditions connect the philosopher Nagarjuna with the place as well, though the sources don't agree. Fourth, the library.

teach.h: DHARMAGANJA: THE TREASURY OF THE DHARMA.
teach.b: Tibetan accounts give it a name, Dharmaganja, the treasury of the dharma, and name the buildings that held its books: Ratnasagara, ocean of jewels, and others.

Whatever its exact size, here texts were copied, kept, argued over and carried away by students who went home to other lands. Much of what later traveled to Tibet and China passed through places like this.
A library is a strange kind of treasure. It keeps nothing for itself. It only works when someone opens it, learns, and carries the learning somewhere else.

how: Tibetan Buddhist traditions describe their own monastic study, with memorization and formal debate, as carrying on the Nalanda tradition, and remember the Nalanda masters in their lineages.

games.q: you've traveled a long way to Nalanda. at the gate a monk asks you a hard question about the teaching. what happens next?
o: you show a letter from a king and walk in.
you answer, and only if you answer well do you get in.
you pay a fee to the gatekeeper.
games.why: in Xuanzang's account, the keepers of the gate tested newcomers with questions, and those who couldn't answer went home.

practice: Bring to mind one question you've wondered about and never looked into, a word, a place, how something works, and hold it the way a newcomer at Nalanda's gate might, as something worth getting through a gate for.
Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Nalanda. The monastery in northern India that worked like a university, where teachers and students from many lands studied, debated and kept a great library.
